title: ICT Paper 1 · Foundational (Robots + Flowcharts & Scratch)
instructions: Theory (40) then Practical (20). Marks in [brackets] tell you how many points to write: a 3-mark question needs 3 separate points. Use the correct ICT words. Flowcharts: pencil and ruler, label every decision arrow Yes/No. Scratch questions: build in Scratch, then describe your blocks in the answer box or upload a screenshot.

questions.prompt: A robot is best described as:
options: any machine that has a motor
a programmable machine that completes a task by replacing human effort
a computer that thinks like a human
a toy that looks like a person

questions.prompt: The field of study focused on developing robots and automation is called:
Which part of a robot is known as its "brain"?
Actuators are like a robot's:
Which sensor tells a robot how close an object is?
A robot built with a head, torso, arms and legs is called a:
Which of these is a non-humanoid robot?
options: a robot with a human-like face that talks
a robotic arm that bolts wheels onto cars
a robot that walks on two legs
a robot shaped like a person that greets visitors

questions.prompt: Making microprocessors is an example of which type of task?
Sojourner, the robot sent to explore Mars, is an example of a robot doing:
Once a robot has been programmed, when is a human needed?
options: to give the robot a rest
to remind it of the steps every hour
only if the robot develops a fault

questions.prompt:
Word box (some words are NOT used): programmable · humanoid · sensors · controller · actuators · repetitive · bumpers · chemicals · dangerous · cameras

Robots are ________ machines.
________ give a robot information about its surroundings.
________ tell a robot that it has collided with something.
Bolting 8,000 wheels onto cars every day is an example of a ________ task.
Sensors that detect ________ give a robot its sense of smell and taste.
A robot must look like a human.
A robot can think and make its own decisions, just like a human.
questions.explanation: Handout: a robot cannot think like a human; it carries out whatever instructions it has been programmed to do.

questions.prompt: Video cameras give a robot sight.
Robots are used under the sea to inspect and repair oil rigs.
A robot gets tired and bored if it does the same job many times.

Match each part (a–e) to its job (i–v). Write e.g. a–iv.
Column A: a. Controller · b. Actuator · c. Pressure sensor · d. Proximity sensor · e. Video camera
Column B: i. Lets the robot know it is touching something · ii. Gives the robot sight · iii. Tells the robot how close an object is · iv. Gets input from sensors, makes decisions and sends commands · v. Converts energy into motion, like a muscle
What is a robot?
questions.answer: A programmable machine that completes a task by replacing human effort.
markScheme: Must say programmable/programmed. 'A machine that does work' = 0.

questions.prompt: Give two reasons why a robot is better than a human at a repetitive job, such as bolting wheels onto cars.
questions.answer: Any two: does not get bored; does not get tired; no mistakes from tiredness; does not get injured; works continuously / the same way every time.
markScheme: Two versions of the same idea = 1 mark only

questions.prompt: State two differences between a humanoid robot and a non-humanoid robot.
questions.answer: Humanoid looks like/mimics a human (head, torso, arms, legs); non-humanoid does not. Humanoid is built to interact/work alongside humans; non-humanoid is shaped for a specific task or environment.
markScheme: Each difference must compare BOTH types
'Humanoid looks like a human' alone = half at most

questions.prompt: Give one example of each: a humanoid robot and a non-humanoid robot.
questions.answer: Humanoid: ASIMO, Sophia, any human-shaped robot. Non-humanoid: robotic arm in a car factory, robot vacuum, Mars rover (Sojourner).

questions.prompt: "A robot vacuum cleaner keeps crashing into furniture and does not avoid obstacles." Which part of the robot is most likely not working?
Explain how the robot vacuum should avoid the furniture when it is working properly. Use the words sensor, controller and actuator.
questions.answer: The sensor detects the furniture/obstacle → the controller receives this input and decides to change direction → the controller sends a command to the actuators/motors, which turn or stop the robot.
markScheme: 1 mark for each component correctly placed in the chain sensor → controller → actuator
If the actuator 'decides', no mark for that link

questions.prompt: "A robot in a laboratory is programmed to mix chemicals. One day, because of a mistake in its program, it mixes the wrong chemicals." The robot did not notice or correct its own mistake. Why not?
questions.answer: A robot cannot think for itself / cannot guess (1); it follows its program exactly, even when the program is wrong (1).

questions.prompt: Give one reason why a robot, rather than a human, is used to mix chemicals in a laboratory.
questions.answer: Chemicals can be dangerous/harmful to humans (1) — the robot can work in an unsafe environment without being hurt (1). Also accept: more accurate at measuring (detailed work).

questions.prompt: Draw the flowchart symbol for each, and name it: (a) Start / Stop (b) Input / Output (c) A question or condition to check.
markScheme: 1 mark each: shape drawn AND named

questions.prompt: Draw a flowchart to convert hours into minutes: input hours (variable 'hours'), calculate minutes = hours * 60, display minutes.
questions.answer: Start (oval) → Input hours (parallelogram) → minutes = hours * 60 (rectangle) → Display minutes (parallelogram) → Stop (oval), with arrows.

questions.prompt: A program asks for today's temperature. If it is greater than 30 it displays "Hot day", otherwise "Cool day". Draw the flowchart (label Yes and No).
questions.answer: Start → Input temperature (parallelogram) → Is temperature > 30? (diamond) → Yes: Display "Hot day" / No: Display "Cool day" (parallelograms) → Stop.
markScheme: 1 diamond with correct condition AND Yes/No labelled
1 both outputs on the correct branches, leading to Stop

questions.prompt: Convert your flowchart into a Scratch program. List the blocks you used in order (or upload a screenshot). What does the sprite say for 35? For 20?
questions.answer: when green flag clicked → ask [Enter the temperature] and wait → if <(answer) > 30> then say [Hot day] else say [Cool day]. 35 → Hot day, 20 → Cool day.
markScheme: 1 both say blocks in the correct slots
Two separate if blocks that work = 2/3

questions.prompt: Flowchart: Start → counter = 1 → Is counter <= 3? → Yes: Print counter * 2 → counter = counter + 1 → back to the question. No → Stop. Write everything it prints, in order.
markScheme: 2 marks all three in order; 1 mark for two correct values

questions.prompt: How many times will the Print step run?
Build a Scratch program that asks for the user's name, then makes the sprite say the name exactly 3 times, 1 second each, using a loop. List your blocks in order (or upload a screenshot).
questions.answer: when green flag clicked → ask [What is your name?] and wait → repeat (3) { say (answer) for (1) seconds }
markScheme: 1 say answer for 1 second inside the loop
Three separate say blocks with no loop = 1/3 max; 'forever' = 0 for the loop mark

questions.prompt: Scratch has three loop blocks: repeat, repeat until and forever. Which one did you use, and why is it the best choice?
questions.answer: Repeat (repeat X times) — because we know exactly how many times the action must happen (3).
markScheme: Must give the reason, not just name the block
